power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("P = 0.44", "p > 0.05"), Sentence = c("The minimum sample size was calculated using Cochran's formula (Z = 1.96, P = 0.44, d = 0.05), yielding n = 379.", "Caregiver sex, child sex, residence, burn type, transport, first responder, distance to the 155 facility, caregiver age and child age were not significantly associated with management outcome 156 (p > 0.05)." )), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

text.text: The study was designed to inform targeted interventions for early pediatric burn care in Zambia and similar settings.

This cross-sectional analytical study was conducted at three health facilities in Mazabuka District, Southern Province, Zambia: Mazabuka General Hospital (the principal district referral facility), Kaonga Mini Hospital, and Nakambala Urban Clinic.
Mazabuka District lies approximately 127 km south of Lusaka and has a population of slightly over 250,000 (ZamStats, 2022 Census).
The facilities collectively serve urban and peri-urban populations and represent the main points of first clinical contact for pediatric burn injuries in the district.
Data were collected between 25 September and 14 December 2025.
The study is reported in line with STROBE [12].

text.text: The sample comprised primary caregivers and their children aged 0-15 years presenting with superficial burns within seven days of injury.
Caregivers of children with deep partial or fullthickness burns, those presenting without a caregiver, and those who declined consent were excluded.
The minimum sample size was calculated using Cochran's formula (Z = 1.96, P = 0.44, d = 0.05), yielding n = 379.
Participants were recruited by systematic sampling: based on an anticipated number of eligible episodes, every third eligible caregiver presenting at any of the three facilities was invited.
Respondents were primary caregivers of children aged 0-15 years, with the children serving as index patients.

text.text: The questionnaire captured caregiver sociodemographic characteristics, burn-event details, prehospital care practices, health-seeking behaviour, transport and distance to facility, and caregiver beliefs regarding traditional remedies.
In addition, a standardised clinical record abstraction form was used to extract burn characteristics and clinical status at arrival from patient medical records.
Following stabilisation of the injured child, eligible caregivers were approached by trained research assistants and interviewed in the local language using password-protected tablet devices.
Daily completeness and consistency checks were conducted throughout the data-collection period.
The pre-test involved approximately 20 caregivers at the same three Mazabuka facilities to check language, flow, and timing; those interviews were excluded from the analysis, and items were revised.
The primary outcome was prehospital burn wound management, classified as good or poor.

Poor management was defined as failure to cool the burn with running water for at least 20 minutes cover the wound with a clean dressing and/or apply harmful substances (e.g., butter, oil, toothpaste, ash, or herbal preparations) before facility presentation.

Most families lived in urban areas (85.5%, n=288/337) and were within 5 km of the facility (86.6%, n=292/337).

text.text: Urban residence was 165 associated with lower odds of good management compared to rural residence (AOR 0.22; 95% CI: 166 0.05-0.92).
Each additional year of caregiver age was associated with slightly lower odds (AOR 167 0.92; 95% CI: 0.86-0.98).
Conversely, each additional year of child age was associated with 168 higher odds of good management (AOR 1.25; 95% CI: 1.10-1.43).
Finally, each additional minute 169 taken to reach the facility was associated with lower odds of good management (AOR 0.96; 95% 170 CI: 0.94-0.98).
No other variable reached statistical significance in the adjusted model.
171 Although most caregivers reported providing first aid, only 13% met our definition of good care.
This gap between reported practice and recommended care may reflect incomplete knowledge, competing beliefs, or both.
Caregivers with belief in traditional remedies were significantly more likely to be in the poor management group.

Similar findings were reported in studies from Malawi and South Africa, where many caregivers either provided no pre-hospital burn care or relied on traditional remedies due to cultural beliefs, misconceptions, and limited knowledge of appropriate burn first aid [17, 18].

text.text: In Malawi and other African countries, eggs, oil, honey, toothpaste, and herbal mixtures are frequently applied to burns because they are believed to prevent blisters or promote healing [17, 18, 20].

However, caregivers with poor management were more likely to view traditional remedies as appropriate than those with good management.
These beliefs are passed down through families and communities rather than taught by health workers [18].

text.text: The social legitimacy of traditional remedies makes it hard for health messages from clinics to change behavior quickly.
Studies indicate that health programs that work with community leaders and respect local beliefs may be more successful than those that simply provide information about correct techniques [18, 21].

text.text: Urban residence alone may not ensure appropriate prehospital burn care, as caregiver knowledge, beliefs, and access to accurate burn first-aid information appear to be more important determinants of practice than place of residence.
Therefore, burn first-aid education should target both urban and rural populations [27].

text.text: In our study, urban residence was associated with lower adjusted odds of good management than rural residence, although most participants were urban (85.5%).
Our study found that older caregivers were less likely to provide good prehospital wound management.

Our study adds useful, real-world evidence from a Zambian district where little is published on how burns are managed before reaching a health facility, helping to fill an important gap in the region.
The study recruited patients from three facilities which strengthens the reliability of the findings.

That said, the results should be interpreted with caution because our study was crosssectional and cannot establish causality, and the reliance on self-reported practices may have introduced social desirability bias, whereby some caregivers may have overstated their adherence to recommended childcare practices [29]In addition, our study included only those who came to health facilities, likely missing those with the poorest care practices, and did not capture factors like income, health literacy, or the exact home treatments used, which limits how fully the results can explain what is happening in practice.

Separation in the multivariable model was driven by 44 good-management events, not by treating sample size as the outcome count.
Good prehospital management of pediatric superficial burns was uncommon in Mazabuka District, with only 13% of children receiving appropriate care.

Children brought to health facilities sooner, older children, and those from rural areas were more likely to receive good care, whereas older caregivers and urban residence were associated with poorer care.
Community education should emphasise cooling burns under clean, cool running water for 20 minutes, avoiding harmful substances, and promptly seeking medical care.
Health education sessions at child health clinics and targeted community outreach for older caregivers and urban households may improve prehospital burn management.
